content: Caltha palustris, commonly referred to as Kingcup or Marsh Marigold, is a member of the Ranunculaceae family. It is native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe (such as Iceland and Arctic Russia), temperate and Arctic Asia, and North America. This plant thrives in wet, boggy environments like marshes, fens, ditches, and wet woodlands. It grows most luxuriantly in partially shaded areas but is rarely found on peat soils. In the United Kingdom, it is considered one of the most ancient native plants, having survived glaciations and flourished in landscapes inundated with glacial meltwaters after the last ice retreat. Caltha palustris is a herbaceous perennial plant that can grow up to 80 cm in height. Its leaves are rounded to kidney-shaped, measuring 3–20 cm across, with bluntly serrated edges and a thick, waxy texture. The stems of the plant are hollow. The flowers are bright yellow, measuring 2–5 cm in diameter, and typically have 4–9 petaloid sepals (most commonly 5) and numerous yellow stamens. These flowers bloom from early spring to late summer and are visited by a wide variety of insects for pollen and nectar. The nectar is secreted from small depressions located on either side of each carpel. The carpels develop into green, sac-like follicles up to 1 cm long, which open to release multiple seeds. Caltha palustris is a highly polymorphic species, exhibiting continuous and independent variation in many of its characteristics. In the UK, it can be divided into two subspecies: Caltha palustris subsp. palustris and Caltha palustris subsp. minor. In clayey garden soils, it is sometimes considered a weed, as every fragment of its root can survive and propagate. However, in warm, free-draining soils, the plant tends to die off. Like many members of the Ranunculaceae family, all parts of the plant can be irritant or toxic. Excessive handling of the plant has been reported to cause skin rashes and dermatitis. In the UK, Caltha palustris is known by various common names depending on the region. These include Marsh Marigold and Kingcup (the two most frequently used names), as well as Mayflower, May Blobs, Mollyblobs, Pollyblobs, Horse Blob, Water Blobs, Water Bubbles, Gollins, and The Publican. The name marigold is derived from its historical use in churches during medieval times at Easter as a tribute to the Virgin Mary, hence Mary gold. The specific epithet palustris comes from the Latin term meaning of a marsh, reflecting its typical habitat. Richard Mabey, in his book Flora Britannica, describes Marsh Marigolds as plants in decline due to agricultural land drainage. However, he notes their robust, three-dimensional appearance, with fleshy leaves and shiny petals that stand out against frostbitten grasses. Many of the plant's surviving local names, such as water-blobs and molly-blobs, reflect its solid, rounded form, with the name The Publican from Lancashire being particularly notable. In North America, Caltha palustris is also known as Cowslip, though this should not be confused with Primula veris, the original plant associated with that name. The plant is frequently mentioned in literature, including works by Shakespeare. It also features in the children’s book Kingcup Cottage by Racey Helps. The 2006–2007 edition of the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Plant Finder, a British publication listing over 70,000 plants available in UK nurseries, includes the following varieties and cultivars of Caltha palustris: Caltha palustris (awarded the RHS Award of Garden Merit) Caltha palustris var. alba Caltha palustris var. barthei Caltha palustris 'Flore Pleno' (a double-flowered cultivar, also awarded the RHS Award of Garden Merit) Caltha palustris var. himalensis Caltha palustris 'Marilyn' Caltha palustris 'Multiplex' (double-flowered) Caltha palustris var. palustris Caltha palustris var. palustris 'Plena' (double-flowered) Caltha palustris subsp. polypetala
